title: Waves and resonance
question: What are waves and resonance?

principle.name: Waves and resonance
principle.formulaNote: wave speed = frequency × wavelength, so for a fixed speed a higher frequency means shorter waves; and a system pushed at its own natural frequency resonates
principle.idea: A wave is a wobble that travels, carrying energy but not the stuff it moves through, and its speed is how many waves pass each second times the length of each one: v = f × λ. Push anything at its own natural rhythm and small pushes add up to a big swing: that is resonance.
principle.discovered: 1636 · Marin Mersenne, France: the laws of vibrating strings and the first measured frequency of a musical note

examples.title: A piano string's note
examples.text: The A above middle C vibrates 440 times a second, so its sound wave in the room is 343 ÷ 440 = 78 cm long. A string's length, tension and weight set its speed of waves, and so its pitch.

examples.title: Frets on a guitar
examples.text: A plucked string rings with standing waves at fₙ = n v ÷ 2L: 82, 165, 247 Hz… for the low E. Press the 12th fret, halve L, and the note jumps an octave.

examples.title: A flute's air column
examples.text: Open at both ends, the air inside follows the same rule as a string with v = 343 m/s. About 66 cm of air gives C4 at 262 Hz; blow harder and it jumps to the second harmonic.

examples.title: The tabla's black spot
examples.text: A plain drumhead's overtones are out of tune. The tabla's heavy syahi reshapes its vibrations so they fall into a musical series, as C. V. Raman showed in 1920.

examples.title: Your cochlea
examples.text: The membrane inside your inner ear is stiff at one end and floppy at the other, so each place resonates with its own pitch: high notes near the entrance, low notes at the tip.

examples.title: Microwave hot spots
examples.text: At 2.45 GHz the waves are c ÷ f = 12.2 cm long, and bouncing between the walls they make hot spots about 6 cm apart. The door's 1–2 mm holes are far smaller than that, so microwaves bounce back while light gets out.

examples.title: A washer's spin-up shudder
examples.text: The tub hangs on springs with a natural frequency of a few hertz. As the drum spins up through about 200 rpm, the clothes shake it at resonance; at 1,400 rpm it runs far calmer.

examples.title: MRI is magnetic resonance
examples.text: In a 1.5 tesla magnet, hydrogen nuclei wobble at 63.9 MHz. A radio pulse at exactly that frequency tips them over; any other frequency does almost nothing.

examples.title: Colours on a TV
examples.text: Each pixel mixes red, green and blue light of about 630, 530 and 460 nm. The remote talks to the TV with infrared at about 940 nm, too long a wavelength for your eyes.

examples.title: Light slowing in a lens
examples.text: Light moves about a third slower in glass. Its frequency can't change, so its wavelength shrinks and the wavefront swings round: that bend is how a camera lens focuses.

hook: Shake a rope, pluck a string, switch on a microwave: it's the same rule every time, speed = frequency × wavelength. Play with waves on a rope, in air and in light, push a swing and a washing machine into resonance, and find out what really brought down the Tacoma Narrows Bridge.

explainer.title: A wave carries energy, not stuff
explainer.text: Shake a rope and a shape runs along it while each bit of rope only goes up and down. Each shake sends one wavelength, so v = f × λ. The speed belongs to the rope; shaking faster only packs the crests closer.

explainer.title: Sound is squeezed air
explainer.text: A loudspeaker pushes air into bunches that race away at 343 m/s. Pitch is frequency: A4 is 440 Hz with 78 cm waves. A string or pipe fixed at its ends rings only at fₙ = n v ÷ 2L, the harmonics.

explainer.title: Light is a wave too
explainer.text: Radio, microwaves, light and X-rays are electromagnetic waves, all at c. A microwave oven's 2.45 GHz waves are 12.2 cm long, making hot spots 6 cm apart, and the door's tiny holes turn them back while light gets out.

explainer.title: Resonance: push in step
explainer.text: Everything that can wobble has a natural frequency. Push at that rhythm, like a swing every 3 s, and small pushes add up until damping balances them. Washers shudder as they spin through it; a wine glass can shatter.

explainer.title: Surprises and a myth
explainer.text: Waves add, so they can cancel: calm lines between ripples, beats between close notes. Sound needs a medium, light doesn't. And Tacoma Narrows wasn't simple resonance: a steady wind fed a twisting flutter.

concepts.def: How many waves pass a point each second, in hertz (Hz).
The distance from one crest to the next.
How fast the pattern travels: v = f × λ. Set by the medium, not the source.
Two waves travelling opposite ways that add into a pattern of fixed nodes and antinodes.
The whole-number multiples of a string's or pipe's lowest frequency: fₙ = n v ÷ 2L.
Linked electric and magnetic fields travelling at c = 299,792 km/s, even through empty space.
A large response when a system is driven at its own natural frequency.
Waves adding where they overlap: reinforcing in step, cancelling half a wave out of step.
